question: According to a recent update from the Hellenic Fertilizers’ Association (SPEL), the full implementation of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) from 1 January 2026 creates unprecedented uncertainty in the fertiliser market and directly threatens the competitiveness of European agriculture.

Businesses are required to institute it in 2026 and pay the unknown cost of the CBAM in 2027, while the necessary benchmarks, emission certification rules and reference price of the Emissions Trading System (ETS) have not yet been published. The 20–30 % charge envisaged (e.g.

EUR 98–130/tonne for urea) will be passed on to farmers, threatening the sustainability of harvests, especially in countries such as Greece that are already facing acute liquidity shortages. In view of the above: 1.
How does the Commission intend to address the issue of complete price uncertainty, which makes it impossible to plan the fertiliser market before the implementation of the CBAM?
Does the Commission intend to consider a postponement or a transition period for the fertiliser sector, as well as the establishment of a ‘locked’ ETS price for the purposes of the CBAM?
Is the Commission planning support measures for farmers who will bear the increased production costs and are at risk of abandoning crops?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.2.2026) In December 2025, the Commission adopted the detailed rules for the definitive phase of the carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM)1 including the methodology for calculating embedded emissions, default values and the rules for the free allocation adjustment. This allows the calculation of the CBAM obligation for imported fertilisers.

The CBAM Regulation2 provides that the definitive phase of the CBAM commences on 1 January 2026. No postponement is foreseen. The price of CBAM certificates is derived from the quarterly price of allowances auctioned under the EU Emissions Trading System. To provide further clarity, the Commission will calculate and publish the quarterly price applying to the respective previous quarter as soon as possible.

The Commission is taking several steps to support farmers. Given the impact of high fertiliser prices, under CBAM, it has recently introduced a lower, 1% mark-up for the default values that may be used to calculate the CBAM obligation for fertilisers.
The Commission is also suggesting a temporary suspension of the Most-Favoured-Nation tariff for ammonia, urea and other fertilisers, if needed, from countries other than Russia or Belarus.

Furthermore, in its legislative proposal amending the CBAM Regulation3, the Commission has included a measure that would allow for the temporary suspension of the application of CBAM for specific goods, as a safeguard in case of unforeseen circumstances4.

Lastly, the Commission is monitoring the availability and affordability of fertilisers in the EU through the Fertilisers Market Observatory and will, in the first half of 2026, propose an action plan for fertilisers5.
